```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

devtools::load_all("..", quiet = TRUE)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Purpose and completion criteria

Assess whether the current simulator can reproduce the supplied demographic schedules of fertility and mortality over the simulation period adequately for milestone 1. For this assessment, the input fertility and mortality rates will be held constant across the simulation. 

To make this assessment, I will replicate 100 simulations with the same input values and compare means of output measures to input measures. I will also repeat this process for different demographic profiles of fertility and mortality. 

| Measure | Comparison | Acceptance criterion |
|---|---|---|
| ASFR | Output births / female exposure versus input rates | 95% CI of mean ASFR for each age group and time period falls includes true input ASFR |
| TFR | Output versus input TFR over matched ages | 95% CI of mean TFR across iterations includes true input TFR for all time increments |
| ASMR | Output deaths / exposure versus input rates, by sex | 95% CI of mean ASFR for each age group and time period falls includes true input ASFR |
| Life expectancy | Output versus input-derived life table | 95% CI of mean TFR across iterations includes true input TFR for all time increments |
| Birth spacing and accounting | Existing tests and checks on simulated histories | Successful unit tests |

Our primary measure of acceptance will be that the true values for each measure fall within the 95% confidence interval of the mean estimate from the simulation. However, because we will be performing this test for a large number of points, we do expect that not every point will fall within that 95% CI. 

## Inputs and simulation design

```{r}
#| label: set-settings

# country to pull HFD/HMD data
country <- "USA"
# year to pull HFD/HMD data and also the beginning year of sim
start_time <- 2000
# years to run simulation
years <- 100
# ending time of the simulation
end_time <- start_time + years
# initial population construction parameters
population_size <- 100000
max_age <- 100
# minimum birth interval in years (0.75 = 9 months)
birth_interval <- 0.75
# seeds for random processes
population_seed <- 42
replication_seeds <- seq_len(100)
```

### Prepare inputs

Fertility and mortality rates come from the Human Fertility Database and Human Mortality Database, respectively. The open-ended categories for under 13 and over 55 for fertility are excluded. 

```{r}
#| label: prepare-inputs

mortality_rates <- get_mortality_hmd(country, start_time)
fertility_rates <- get_fertility_hfd(country, start_time)

input_tfr <- calculate_tfr(fertility_rates)
input_life_table <- calculate_life_table(mortality_rates)
input_life_expectancy <- input_life_table |>
  filter(age_start == 0) |>
  select(sex, ex)

input_tfr
input_life_expectancy
```

### Initialization and observation windows

All replications below share one baseline population. They measure simulation
variability conditional on that population. Baseline-generation variability
would require a separate design.

Because of the arbitrary nature of the initial population, there will typically be a "burn-in" period before a stable population is achieved. Measures based on ASMR and ASFR still should be valid throughout, but population growth may be highly variable. However, because the simulation modifies actual fertility rates to account for non-exposure of pregnant mothers, the initial ASFR and TFR estimates will be slightly higher because all women start out as non-pregnant.

```{r}
#| label: construct-model
set.seed(population_seed)
population <- create_baseline_population(
  population_size, max_age = max_age, end_time = start_time
)
model <- hammel_model() |>
  set_population(population) |>
  set_mortality(mortality_rates) |>
  set_fertility(fertility_rates, birth_interval = birth_interval)

fertility_time_breaks <- c(
  seq(start_time, start_time + 9, 1),
  seq(start_time + 10, end_time, 10)
)
mortality_time_breaks <- seq(start_time, end_time, 10)
# Finite last breakpoints automatically gain an open interval.
life_table_age_breaks <- 0:100
mortality_age_breaks <- 0:110
fertility_age_breaks <- sort(unique(c(
  0, fertility_rates$age_start, fertility_rates$age_end
)))
```

## Replications and demographic extraction

The simulation is run 100 times and for each run, I calculate the lexis diagram to get person years, births, and deaths within given time and range brakets.

```{r}
#| label: run-replications
results <- map(replication_seeds, function(seed) {
  simulate(model, years = years, seed = seed)
})
names(results) <- as.character(replication_seeds)

fertility_counts <- map(results, calculate_lexis_counts,
  time_breaks = fertility_time_breaks,
  age_breaks = fertility_age_breaks)
mortality_counts <- map(results, calculate_lexis_counts,
  time_breaks = mortality_time_breaks,
  age_breaks = mortality_age_breaks)
life_table_counts <- map(results, calculate_lexis_counts,
  time_breaks = fertility_time_breaks,
  age_breaks = life_table_age_breaks)

tfr <- map(fertility_counts, calculate_tfr) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "replication") |>
  mutate(time_mid = (time_start + time_end) / 2) |>
  select(replication, time_mid, tfr)
asfr <- bind_rows(fertility_counts, .id = "replication") |>
  filter(sex == "f") |>
  mutate(time_mid = (time_start + time_end) / 2,
         age_mid = (age_start + age_end) / 2) |>
  select(replication, time_mid, age_mid, asfr) |>
  filter(age_mid >= 13 & age_mid < 55)
asmr <- bind_rows(mortality_counts, .id = "replication") |>
  mutate(time_mid = (time_start + time_end) / 2,
         age_mid = (age_start + age_end) / 2) |>
  select(replication, time_mid, age_mid, sex, asmr)
life_expectancy <- map(life_table_counts, calculate_life_table) |>
  bind_rows(.id = "replication") |>
  mutate(time_mid = (time_start + time_end) / 2) |>
  filter(age_start == 0) |>
  select(replication, time_mid, sex, ex)
```

## Fertility results

### Total fertility rate

```{r}
#| label: fig-tfr-comparison
#| fig-cap: Mean TFR across 100 simulations by time period. Grey ribbon shows 95% confidence interval for the sample mean. Dotted line shows the true TFR based on the input age-specific fertility rates.

tfr_summary <- tfr |>
  group_by(time_mid) |>
  summarize(
    mean = mean(tfr),
    sd = sd(tfr),
    n = n(),
    se = sd / sqrt(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(tfr_summary, aes(x = time_mid, y = mean))+
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se), 
              color = NA, fill = "grey")+
  geom_line(color = "navy")+
  geom_point(color = "navy")+
  geom_hline(yintercept = input_tfr$tfr, linetype = 2, color = "tomato")+
  labs(x = "year", y = "Mean TFR")+
  theme_bw()
```

@fig-tfr-comparison shows the mean TFR in each time period across the 100 replicated simulations. To account for the potential bias in the early simulation due to a lack of pregnant woman, I use one year time periods for the first decade and then ten year periods for the remainder of the simulation. 

As expected, there is some upward bias initially due to the fertility adjustments. However, this bias is removed after the first two years of the simulation. Every remaining estimate's 95% confidence interval contains the true TFR and there is no evidence of a trend. 

### Age-specific fertility rates

```{r}
#| label: fig-asfr-comparison
#| fig-cap: The figure shows age specific fertility rates from the input data in red and a 95% confidence interval for the mean of the age-specific fertility rates across 100 simulations, separately by time period.

asfr_summary <- asfr |>
  group_by(time_mid, age_mid) |>
  summarize(
    mean = mean(asfr),
    sd = sd(asfr),
    n = n(),
    se = sd / sqrt(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(asfr_summary, aes(x = age_mid, y = mean))+
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se), 
              color = NA, fill = "grey20")+
  #geom_line(color = "navy")+
  geom_line(data = fertility_rates, aes(x = age_start + 0.5, y = rate),
            color = "tomato", alpha = 0.5)+
  facet_wrap(~time_mid)+
  labs(x = "age (mid-point)", y = "age-specific fertility rate")+
  theme_bw()
```

@fig-asfr-comparison shows a very close comparison between the estimated age-specific fertility rates across simulations and the input rates. The only differences are again in the first two years, where the estimated rates are slightly higher, as expected. 

## Mortality results

### Life expectancy

Because of sparsity over age 100, it is difficult to calculate life expectancy on life tables that extend to an open interval at 110+ years, consistent with the input data from HMD. Therefore, I truncate the open ended interval here to 100, which may lead to a slight systematic bias relative to the life expectancy estimated directly from the HMD data. However, given that mortality is high and flattens out in this period, the bias is likely to be very small.

```{r}
#| label: fig-le-comparison
#| fig-cap: Mean life expectancy at age zero across 100 simulations by time period. Grey ribbon shows 95% confidence interval for the sample mean. Dotted line shows the true life expectancy based on the input age-specific mortality rates.

life_exp_summary <- life_expectancy |>
  group_by(time_mid, sex) |>
  summarize(
    mean = mean(ex),
    sd = sd(ex),
    n = sum(!is.na(ex)),
    se = sd / sqrt(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(life_exp_summary, aes(x = time_mid, y = mean))+
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se), 
              color = NA, fill = "grey")+
  geom_line(color = "navy")+
  geom_point(color = "navy")+
  geom_hline(data = input_life_expectancy, aes(yintercept = ex), linetype = 2)+
  facet_wrap(~sex, scales = "free_y")+
  labs(x = "year", y = "Mean Life Expectancy at Age Zero")+
  theme_bw()
```

@fig-le-comparison shows how well the empirically estimated life expectancy fits to the life expectancy of the input mortality rates, separately by gender. In general, it fits very well. Only one estimate's 95% confidence interval does not include the true input life expectancy, but this is quite plausibly a random error given the number of data points tested. I observe no trend here, nor any initial difficulty in the "burn in" period.

### Age-specific mortality rates

```{r}
#| label: fig-asmr-comparison-male
#| fig-cap: The figure shows male age specific mortality rates from the input data in red and a 95% confidence interval for the mean of the age-specific mortality rates across 100 simulations, separately by time period. Truncated at age 100 due to very small sample sizes at higher ages.

asmr_summary <- asmr |>
  group_by(time_mid, age_mid, sex) |>
  summarize(
    mean = mean(asmr, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(asmr, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(asmr)),
    se = sd / sqrt(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

asmr_summary |>
  filter(sex == "m") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_mid, y = mean))+
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se), 
              color = NA, fill = "grey20")+
  geom_line(data = filter(mortality_rates, sex == "m"), 
            aes(x = age_start + 0.5, y = rate),
            color = "tomato", alpha = 0.5)+
  facet_wrap(~time_mid)+
  scale_y_log10(limits = c(.00005, .5))+
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100))+
  labs(x = "age (mid-point)", y = "age-specific mortality rate (log scale)")+
  theme_bw()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-asmr-comparison-female
#| fig-cap: The figure shows female age specific mortality rates from the input data in red and a 95% confidence interval for the mean of the age-specific mortality rates across 100 simulations, separately by time period. Truncated at age 100 due to very small sample sizes at higher ages.

asmr_summary |>
  filter(sex == "f") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_mid, y = mean))+
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se), 
              color = NA, fill = "grey20")+
  geom_line(data = filter(mortality_rates, sex == "f"), 
            aes(x = age_start + 0.5, y = rate),
            color = "tomato", alpha = 0.5)+
  facet_wrap(~time_mid)+
  scale_y_log10(limits = c(.00005, .5))+
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100))+
  labs(x = "age (mid-point)", y = "age-specific mortality rate (log scale)")+
  theme_bw()
```

@fig-asmr-comparison-male and @fig-asmr-comparison-female show the fit of male and female age-specific mortality rates, respectively, from the input schedules in comparison to the 95% CI of the mean ASFR for each simulation, across time. The simulated data fit extremely well to the expected input schedules.
